#1  tinkerer_dee  ·  Posted 3 Feb 2025, 21:14
Member since 2022 · 214 posts · Location: somewhere damp
------------------------------------------------------------

Evening all. Long-time lurker, occasional poster, first time asking for proper help.

I bought a 1983 Peugeot road bike last month from an estate sale for £40. It's the white one with the black and gold decals, steel frame (Reynolds 531 main tubes according to the sticker, which is half peeled off). It's been in a garage for at least twenty years judging by the dust and the 1990s parking permit stuck to the top tube. The plan is to strip it, clean it, replace the consumables and ride it to work in the summer.

Everything has come apart beautifully except the seatpost. The post is aluminium, the frame is steel, and it's been there for forty years. You can see where this is going.

What I've tried so far:

1. Penetrating oil. Took the bottom bracket out, turned the frame upside down, poured penetrating oil down the seat tube from below so it could soak into the join, and topped it up morning and evening for a full week. Also sprayed around the top of the seat tube collar. Nothing.
2. Twisting by hand with the saddle still on. Bent the saddle rails. Post didn't move. Saddle was knackered anyway.
3. Heat. Heat gun on the seat lug for about ten minutes, then tried twisting with the saddle clamp. Nothing. I'm nervous about using a blowtorch because of the paint and the decals, and I'm not sure what too much heat does to 531.
4. Freezing spray on the post (to shrink it) while heating the lug. I've seen this recommended for aluminium in steel. Made a satisfying hiss and achieved nothing else.

The post is a fluted one, maybe 25 cm long, I can see about 12 cm above the collar. Seat binder bolt is out. The slot at the back of the seat lug looks normal.

I'm close to just leaving it and buying a saddle that fits the existing post, but the post is too low for me (I'm 6'1") and I need about 6 cm more height.

Any ideas before I do something stupid? Pictures attached.

#2  oldbikeoli  ·  Posted 3 Feb 2025, 21:32
Moderator · 9,812 posts · Location: Ludlow-ish
------------------------------------------------------------

Welcome to the club nobody wants to be in. Seized aluminium post in a steel frame is probably the single most common restoration problem we see on here. The aluminium and steel have reacted (galvanic corrosion) and the white crusty aluminium oxide that's formed in the gap is now basically cement.

Before anyone else says it: please search the forum, there are about forty threads on this. But since you've clearly already tried the basics, carry on, I'll leave this one open.

Good news first: you've done the right things in the right order. Penetrating oil, heat, freeze. Most posts that are going to come out with gentle methods come out at that stage.

Next step most people try is the bench vice method. Take the saddle off, clamp the top of the post (the bit sticking out) in a big bench vice, and use the frame itself as the lever, turning the whole bike around the post. You'll need a big, solid vice bolted to something heavy. Put something soft in the jaws if you want to save the post (you don't).

Be VERY careful not to twist the frame. Hold it by the seat tube and the head tube area, not by the top tube or the rear triangle, otherwise you'll bend something that's much more expensive than a seatpost.

--
Oli · Mod · “It's not hoarding if it's spares.”

Beautiful bike. That's a PX-10's cheaper cousin, I think — if the decals say “Carbolite” on the seat tube, it's not 531, it's their own tubing, but the photos are a bit blurry.

Important thing nobody's mentioned yet: this is a FRENCH bike from 1983. French bikes of that era used their own sizes for everything. Bottom bracket threads, headset, stem diameter, and the seatpost. So when (not if) you get that post out, don't just order a 27.2 mm post because that's “standard”. Measure the inside of the seat tube with a vernier caliper once it's out and clean.

Also, on the heat: 531 is fine with a heat gun. It's brazed at much higher temperatures. The paint is the thing that will suffer. But honestly at £40 I'd sacrifice the paint to save the frame.

--
G · Too many French bikes · Not enough French

#10  velo_mags  ·  Posted 4 Feb 2025, 07:12
Member · 3,301 posts · Location: Yorkshire Dales
------------------------------------------------------------

Morning. I've done six or seven of these over the years. Here's my honest hierarchy, from “nice” to “nuclear”:

1. Penetrating oil, a week or more — done.
2. Heat + freeze — done.
3. Bench vice, frame as lever — next.
4. Ammonia. Aluminium oxide dissolves slowly in household ammonia. Some people swear by it. Smells horrendous, needs good ventilation, and you need to plug the bottom of the seat tube. I've had it work once out of three tries.
5. Cut the post off a few cm above the collar, then use a hacksaw blade (held in a handle or just wrapped in tape) to cut lengthways down the inside of the post, from the top, in two places so you can collapse it inwards and pull out a strip. This is slow and miserable and if you slip you will cut the inside of the seat tube, which on thin-walled 531 is a really bad idea.
6. Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide). Dissolves aluminium. Does NOT dissolve steel. So you cut the post off, plug the bottom of the seat tube, pour in a caustic soda solution, and the aluminium post literally fizzes away over a day or two. Very effective, but it's genuinely dangerous stuff: it will blind you if it splashes in your eyes, burn your skin, and the reaction produces hydrogen gas, so absolutely no flames and do it outdoors. It will also strip paint instantly and damage anything aluminium it touches — so the front derailleur, any alloy parts, all off first.

Personally I'd do 3, then 6. Skip 4 and 5 unless you enjoy suffering.

Also agree with grimpeur re: French sizing.

--
Mags · “Ride more, faff less.” (I faff constantly.)

#12  grimpeur83  ·  Posted 4 Feb 2025, 09:02
------------------------------------------------------------

> the seat tube sticker does say “Tubes Carbolite 103”

Yep. Carbolite 103 was Peugeot's own heat-treated carbon steel. Perfectly decent, a bit heavier than 531. Doesn't change the plan — everything Mags says about caustic soda applies to any steel frame. Steel doesn't care about sodium hydroxide at room temperature. It's the aluminium, the paint and your eyeballs you need to worry about.

The fork having a 531 sticker but the frame not is common on these. Peugeot weren't always consistent and some forks got swapped over the decades.

Member · 640 posts · Location: Normandy (ex-pat)
------------------------------------------------------------

Lovely thread already. Two things from someone who's restored about a dozen French bikes:

First, the decals. Before you do anything with heat or chemicals near the seat lug, photograph every decal from straight on, with a ruler in the shot. Reproduction decal sets for 1980s Peugeots exist, but they're sized for specific frame sizes and years, and having good photos makes ordering the right set much easier. If you're lucky and the paint survives, you won't need them, but you'll be glad of the photos if it doesn't.

Second, a method nobody has mentioned: electrolysis. Some people set up a little electrolysis rig with a battery charger, washing soda solution and a sacrificial steel electrode down the seat tube, to break down the corrosion. I've seen it work on rusted steel parts, but I'm genuinely not sure it does anything useful for aluminium oxide between aluminium and steel, and getting it wrong can pit the steel. I'd put it in the “interesting but unproven” box for this job. Mentioning it only so nobody thinks it was forgotten.

Bon courage.

#13  oldbikeoli  ·  Posted 4 Feb 2025, 09:10
Moderator

Moderator note: I'm going to say this once, very clearly, because this thread will be found by search engines for years.

If you use caustic soda (sodium hydroxide, sold as drain cleaner crystals in some places — check the label is pure sodium hydroxide, not a mix): wear proper goggles (not glasses), long chemical-resistant gloves and long sleeves. Always add the soda to the water, never the water to the soda, because it gets hot. Do it outside, away from children, pets and anything you'd mind being ruined. Keep a bucket of clean water nearby for splashes. Dispose of the spent solution properly — check what your local council says. Don't seal the top of the seat tube while it's reacting because of the hydrogen.

And if you're not comfortable with any of that, take it to a bike shop. There's no shame in it. A good old-school shop will have done this before.

Right, carry on.

Update. Borrowed my neighbour Rhys's enormous engineering vice (bolted to his workbench, which is bolted to his garage wall, which is bolted to the planet). Took the saddle and clamp off. Clamped the post as tight as the vice would go, with the frame upright, and started to turn the frame, holding it by the seat tube and head tube like Oli said.

Result: the post twisted. The FRONT of it. The top 5 cm that was in the vice twisted about 30 degrees and then sheared through the flutes and tore. The bit inside the frame did not move at all. So now I have a seatpost that's in two pieces: a mangled stub in the vice, and the rest of it still stuck in the frame with about 7 cm of jagged aluminium sticking out of the collar.

Rhys found this very funny. I found it less funny.

So I guess the vice method is officially a fail. On to the nuclear options?

One thing worth doing before you go to caustic: try the ammonia for a few days. It's less dangerous than sodium hydroxide, and I've had more luck than Mags with it — two out of two, although both were posts that had already been loosened a bit by twisting. Your twisting might have cracked the oxide layer. Plug the bottom of the seat tube with a cork wrapped in cling film, fill from the top with household ammonia, cover the top loosely, leave it in the shed for three or four days, then try again with the stub in the vice.

You'll want to stay out of the shed while it's working. It's eye-watering.

#22  grimpeur83  ·  Posted 7 Feb 2025, 11:15
------------------------------------------------------------

> what diameter post am I going to need for the replacement?

For a Peugeot of that age with Carbolite 103 tubing, the seat tube takes a 26.4 mm post. That's the classic French size, and it's slightly under the 26.6 and 26.8 sizes you'll see on some Italian and Japanese frames of the same era. Your measurement of the old post (26.3–26.4) fits perfectly.

Do NOT put a 26.6 in it — people do this all the time because 26.4 is harder to find, and you either can't get it in, or you hammer it in and then you're right back here in 2035 with another seized post.

Good news is that a few companies still make 26.4 mm posts specifically for the vintage French market. Plain (non-fluted) ones in a silver finish look right on a bike like this. Get one at least 250 mm long since you need a lot of extension, and check it has a minimum insertion mark. At 6'1" on what I'm guessing is a 56 cm frame, you'll want plenty in the frame.

When it's in, grease it, or use an anti-seize compound, and take it out and re-grease it once a year. That's the whole secret to never doing this again.

#26  oldbikeoli  ·  Posted 10 Feb 2025, 18:35
Moderator
------------------------------------------------------------

> I think it's caustic soda time.

Respect for exhausting the gentle options first. Reread #13, get proper goggles, and post updates. Strip EVERYTHING off the frame that isn't steel. If the headset cups or bottom bracket cups are alloy, they come out. Mask off or accept losing the paint around the seat lug.

Two more practical tips:
- Don't use a metal bowl or jug to mix it. Use a heavy plastic (polypropylene) container. Caustic soda attacks aluminium cookware, obviously, and some other metals too.
- Mix a fairly strong solution. A common ratio people report is around 100 g of caustic soda per litre of water, but go slowly, it heats up as it dissolves.

------------------------------------------------------------
#27  velo_mags  ·  Posted 10 Feb 2025, 19:00
------------------------------------------------------------

Also: tip the frame upside down so the seat tube is vertical with the open top at the BOTTOM? NO. Other way round. Seat tube vertical, top of the seat tube (where the stub is) at the top. Plug the bottom bracket end of the seat tube with a rubber bung — a wine-bottle stopper or a rubber plumbing bung from a hardware shop — sealed with plenty of silicone or something that won't dissolve. Check it for leaks with plain water first. If it leaks, the soda goes into your bottom bracket shell and out onto your shoes.

Pour the solution in from the top a bit at a time. It will fizz vigorously and get hot. Top it up as it fizzes down. It takes a while — the reaction slows as the solution gets used up, so you'll want to pour it out and add fresh solution a few times.

First post after reading for ages, so hello. I'm a chemistry teacher, so for what it's worth, a few notes on the soda plan, all in support of what Oli and Mags said:

- The reaction is aluminium + sodium hydroxide + water giving sodium aluminate and hydrogen. It's exothermic, which is why the tube gets hot and why it speeds up as it warms and then slows as the soda gets used up. Replacing the solution a few times, like Mags said, is exactly right.
- Hydrogen is lighter than air and disperses fast outdoors, which is why outside is fine and a closed shed or garage is not.
- If you get it on your skin it feels slippery, not burning, at first. That slippery feeling is your skin being dissolved. Rinse with running water for a long time, not a quick splash.
- Eyes: goggles, not glasses. I'll say it again because Oli did. Goggles.

Good luck, Dee. Everyone in my staffroom now knows about your seatpost too.

#32  grimpeur83  ·  Posted 11 Feb 2025, 13:15
------------------------------------------------------------

One more thing before you start, Dee. After the post is gone, there'll be a grey or black sludge left in the tube. That's mostly the alloying elements left behind from the aluminium, and some remaining oxide. Flush the tube thoroughly with lots of water, then dry it with a hair dryer or leave it somewhere warm, then put a light coat of oil or a frame protector spray inside. A steel frame with caustic residue left in it and then left wet will rust from the inside.

And if you have any doubt about whether the frame was damaged — e.g. the seat tube was dented from the vice attempts — take it to someone who can check it before you ride it.

#33  tinkerer_dee  ·  Posted 15 Feb 2025, 17:55
------------------------------------------------------------

Okay. Deep breath. Here's what happened this week.

Prep (Wednesday evening):
- Stripped everything off the frame. Headset cups turned out to be steel but I took them out anyway. Bottom bracket cups out. Rear derailleur hanger is part of the steel dropout so that stayed.
- Cut the remaining stub off as close to the collar as I dared with a junior hacksaw. Probably 3 mm proud. Didn't touch the steel.
- Masked around the seat lug with three layers of thick tape and a bin bag. (Sacrificed the lug paint in my head already.)
- Plugged the bottom of the seat tube with a rubber plumbing bung and a ring of silicone. Let it cure for 24 hours. Tested with water: no leaks. Tipped the water out.
- Bought: 1 kg tub of pure sodium hydroxide from the hardware shop (the label said 99%+ sodium hydroxide), chemical goggles, long nitrile gauntlets, and a polypropylene measuring jug.

The actual job (Thursday and Friday, outside on the patio, kids at school, cat locked in):
- Clamped the frame to a fence post with the seat tube vertical.
- Mixed 100 g of caustic soda into 1 litre of cold water, adding the soda slowly to the water, stirring with a plastic spoon. The jug got properly hot.
- Poured it in from the top, about 200 ml at a time. It fizzed like a bath bomb and a grey froth came up out of the tube. Topped up as it went down.
- After about four hours it had calmed down a lot, so I poured the spent solution into a plastic bucket (the bike upside down, very carefully), and put in fresh solution. Did this three times on Thursday.
- Friday morning I looked down the tube with a torch and could see the post had become a thin, ragged shell. I tapped it with a long screwdriver and a big piece just crumbled away. Did two more rounds of fresh solution in the morning. By Friday lunchtime the last of it was gone. I could see bare steel all the way down to the bung.

After:
- Flushed with about 20 litres of water from the hose, then a bucket of water with a bit of bicarb in it (someone on another thread said this neutralises any leftover, not sure if that's right but it can't hurt), then more hose.
- Dried with a hair dryer for 20 minutes and left it in the airing cupboard overnight.
- Sprayed the inside with frame protector this morning.
- Measured the seat tube with my calipers: 26.4 mm, as grimpeur said. Good call.

So: it's out. The caustic soda did it. Penetrating oil, heat, freezing, the vice, and the ammonia all failed, and the caustic soda dissolved the whole thing in under two days. The paint around the seat lug is a bit blistered under where the tape lifted, but honestly it looks fine and I'll touch it up.

I've ordered a 26.4 mm plain silver post (300 mm) and a tube of anti-seize. And the cat has forgiven me.

Thank you everyone. Especially Oli for the safety lecture, which I read four times.
